runs.question: How does the NIST Generative AI Profile describe data privacy risks?

answer.text:
The NIST Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) treats data privacy as one of its twelve GAI risk areas, in Section 2.4 on pages 11–12. I read those pages directly because the search tool was unavailable.

**Privacy risks from training data.** The profile's core concern is that the use of personal data for GAI training raises risks to widely accepted privacy principles, including to transparency, individual participation (including consent), and purpose speciﬁcation. It adds that most model developers do not disclose speciﬁc data sources on which models were trained, limiting user awareness of whether personally identiﬁably information (PII) was trained on.

**Leakage and memorization.** The profile says models can expose what they were trained on. During adversarial attacks, LLMs have revealed sensitive information (from the public domain) that was included in their training data. It notes this may pose exacerbated privacy risks even for data present only in a small number of training samples.

**Inference of sensitive data.** Models can also reveal information they were never given. They may be able to correctly infer P II or sensitive data that was not in their training data nor disclosed by the user by stitching together information from disparate sources. The profile notes that these inferences can have negative impact on an individual even if the inferences are not accurate (e.g., confabulations).

**Downstream harm.** Beyond exposure, the profile warns that predictive inferences made by GAI models based on PII or protected attributes can contribute to adverse decisions, leading to representational or allocative harms to individuals or groups.

The section also cross-references privacy in its discussion of jailbreaking, noting that output restrictions may fail against novel prompts, which is also relevant to CBRN Information or Capabilities, Data Privacy, Information Security, and Obscene, Degrading and/or Abusive Content.

The profile's suggested actions for managing these risks are in Section 3 (page 16 onward), which I did not read, so I can't summarize its privacy-specific mitigations.

The use of personal data for GAI training raises risks to widely accepted privacy principles, including to transparency, individual participation (including consent), and purpose speciﬁcation.

citations.title: NIST AI 600-1: AI Risk Management Framework, Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, July 2024, page 11
citations.cited_text: For example, most model developers do not disclose speciﬁc data sources on which models were trained, limiting user awareness of whether personally identiﬁably information (PII) was trained on and, if so, how it was collected. Models may leak, generate, or correctly infer sensitive information about individuals.

citations.title: NIST AI 600-1: AI Risk Management Framework, Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, July 2024, page 11
citations.cited_text: For example, during adversarial attacks, LLMs have revealed sensitive information (from the public domain) that was included in their training data. This problem has been referred to as data memorization, and may pose exacerbated privacy risks even for data present only in a small number of training samples.

citations.title: NIST AI 600-1: AI Risk Management Framework, Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, July 2024, page 11
citations.cited_text: In addition to revealing sensitive information in GAI training data, GAI models may be able to correctly infer P II or sensitive data that was not in their training data nor disclosed by the user by stitching together information from disparate sources.

citations.title: NIST AI 600-1: AI Risk Management Framework, Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, July 2024, page 11
citations.cited_text: These inferences can have negative impact on an individual even if the inferences are not accurate (e.g., confabulations), and especially if they reveal information that the individual considers sensitive or that is used to disadvantage or harm them.

citations.title: NIST AI 600-1: AI Risk Management Framework, Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, July 2024, page 11
citations.cited_text: For example, predictive inferences made by GAI models based on PII or protected attributes can contribute to adverse decisions, leading to representational or allocative harms to individuals or groups (see Harmful Bias and Homogenization below).

citations.title: NIST AI 600-1: AI Risk Management Framework, Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, July 2024, page 11
citations.cited_text: Many current systems restrict model outputs to limit certain content or in response to certain prompts, but this approach may still produce harmful recommendations in response to other less-explicit, novel prompts (also relevant to CBRN Information or Capabilities, Data Privacy, Information Security, and Obscene, Degrading and/or Abusive Content).
